# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is a strong follow-up that answers several of the open questions raised by the earlier documents:

- Varden's per-hour gain persists at 24 months, but it has shrunk.
- Hours are now measured from system logs as well as timesheets.
- The meetings hypothesis gets a pre-registered test.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim turns out to rest entirely on uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours.

The main concerns:

1. The Summary compares different measures when it describes the decline.
2. The mediation test is confirmatory in name but runs on the same seven offices that generated the hypothesis, and its confidence intervals look too narrow for 14 clusters.
3. Two control offices changed their own meeting practices, which contaminates the control group, and the meeting figures don't reconcile with that.
4. It isn't clear what the log-based hours actually measure.

## The numbers mostly check out

- **Output per hour:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%** ✓
  - Logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%** ✓
- **Confidence intervals:** both are symmetric on the log scale around their point estimates ✓
- **Halden subset:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4% ✓. Then 96.8 / 0.866 = **+11.8%** ✓
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓

There are two numerical problems:

1. **The Summary overstates the decline by mixing measures.** "Fell from 12.5% … to 8.5%" compares a nine-month timesheet estimate with a 24-month log estimate. The body correctly gives the like-for-like comparison as 12.5% → 9.8%, a fall of 22%. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" is a little generous: a fifth is closer. Mixing the measures implies a 32% decline. No test of the 9- vs 24-month difference is reported, and the two confidence intervals overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is the right wording; "the gain has declined" is stated more firmly than the evidence supports.
2. **The control-office meeting figures don't add up.** Control offices' recurring meetings are reported as 7.2 → 7.0 hours, a fall of 0.2. But two of the seven control offices cut from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. That alone should lower the control mean by about 0.6 hours (2 × 2.1 / 7). For the mean to fall only 0.2, the other five offices must have *increased* their meeting time by about 0.5 hours each, or the mean must be staff-weighted in a way that isn't stated. Either way, it needs explaining.

## What the report does well

- **It meets the standards its critics set.** It uses record-based output, two hours measures, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon. These are exactly the conditions Varga & Holm said would show whether anything remained.
- **The answer is clear.** About 8.5–9.8% remains, with confidence intervals well clear of zero. That rules out "entirely an artifact."
- **It reveals what the meta-analysis didn't.** The four long-run studies the meta-analysis relied on were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. That confirms the main concern about its "no decay" claim.
- **It reports the counter-office outcome plainly**, now with a control comparison (wait of 7.3 vs 4.0 minutes). It also gives a cost estimate for restoring service, which I had noted was missing earlier.
- **It reports a result that cuts against its own case.** The meeting audit in two control offices suggests part of the gain may be available without cutting hours. The authors are careful about what this can and can't show.
- **It labels the Halden subset honestly.** It calls these organisations "survivors twice over" and doesn't present them as general evidence.

## Concerns

### 1. The mediation test is pre-registered but not out-of-sample

Registering the analysis at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes were known, is a real improvement. But the meetings hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices at month six. Re-testing it on the same offices over a longer period guards against analytic flexibility. It does not provide independent replication. So Varga & Holm's warning that findings like this tend not to replicate is only partly answered. The report says the test used "a larger sample of office-months," but the effective sample size for an office-level treatment is still 7 vs 7.

That raises a further problem. A mediation estimate with 14 clusters giving a 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow. The report should say how the intervals account for clustering. If they were computed from office-months as though each month were independent, they are too narrow.

### 2. The mediation model assumes things a cluster trial can't guarantee

The authors note the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. Two specific threats are worth naming:

- **Meetings may stand in for broader management change.** Managers who cut meetings probably also simplified approval steps and protected focus time, the changes described in Halden's interviews. The 47% may be credited to meetings when it partly reflects reorganisation more generally.
- **Part of the meetings effect may be bookkeeping rather than behaviour.** If meetings produce little measured output, cutting them raises output per hour simply by shrinking the denominator. A rough check makes the point. Using timesheets, non-meeting hours were about 29.5 in treated offices against about 30.9 in control, a gap of about 5%. Output per worker was 3.4% lower. That implies a gain of only about 1–2% per non-meeting hour. On that simple accounting, meetings could explain *more* than 47% of the gain. The report should reconcile its mediation model with this direct time accounting.

### 3. It's not clear what log-in hours measure

The report describes log-in time as recording "time staff are working on cases." If it covers only case work, meetings are excluded. Then:

- the mediation pathway through meetings would have to work in a different way;
- the −11% fall in log hours would be hard to square with the timesheet and meeting figures; and
- it would be inaccurate to call the log measure "stricter," since it would simply be measuring something different.

If the logs capture total working time, the description should say so. Either way, the 8.5% figure depends on getting this definition right.

### 4. The control group was contaminated

The meeting audit in two control offices does more than suggest that reorganisation helps. It means part of the treatment's mechanism leaked into the control group from month 15. That probably biases the 24-month treatment effect *downward*, so some of the apparent decline from 9 to 24 months may come from the control offices improving rather than the treated offices fading. The decay estimate should be reported with and without these two offices.

The 4.1% before-after gain in those two offices is uncontrolled, and the audit may have been prompted by a weak period, so some of the gain could be regression to the mean. Still, it is roughly in line with the treated offices' meetings pathway: about 2% per hour of meetings cut, against about 1.2% in treated offices.

### 5. Retrieving baseline meeting data needs explaining

The nine-month report said meeting data were first collected in month six. This report gives baseline values of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. These were presumably reconstructed from calendar history. That is a reasonable method, but it should be stated, along with how complete the historical calendar records were.

### 6. Case-processing outcomes are still incomplete

- **Cost.** Output per FTE is −3.4% at unchanged pay, plus overtime, so cost per case has probably risen by around 4% or more. The report costs the counter arm but not this one.
- **Backlog and timeliness.** As before, the report gives no backlog size or share of cases decided within statutory deadlines. The nine-month report named deadline breaches as a risk to check at follow-up.
- **Quality.** The appeal overturn rate (3.2% vs 3.0%) still has no confidence interval.
- **Output per FTE.** It has moved from −2.1% to −3.4%. The loss per employee may be growing, though the difference is well within the noise.

### 7. Points on the Halden subset

- **More selection.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded, adding another layer of non-response.
- **The work-type split gets blurrier.** A marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. Grouping it under "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the coverage-bound category. Responsiveness to clients is a third form of constraint that the discretionary/coverage-bound split doesn't capture.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** "Likely optimistic" would be more accurate. Survivorship pushes the estimate up, but nothing makes it a true ceiling.

### 8. Overlap between authors and their subjects

The report has a clear interest in its subjects, though it handles this well. The Varden authors are evaluating their own trial and replying to criticism of their own exploratory analysis. Okafor, the Halden lead author, is a co-author on the section about Halden organisations. The report's tone is measured, and it concedes points against itself, such as the gain shrinking and the control-office audit. Still, readers should keep the authorship in mind, especially for how the mediation result is framed.

## Where things now stand

| Question | Best-supported answer after five documents |
|---|---|
| Output per actual hour, discretionary work | About +8–10% at 24 months (Varden logs +8.5%, timesheets +9.8%); about +12% at 9 months |
| Durability | Gain persists to 24 months, with some fading (about −20% like-for-like). This may be partly overstated because of control-office contamination. Beyond 24 months unknown |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | Slightly down, about −2% to −4% (precision limited) |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall. In the one randomised case, the employer abandoned the scheme at 12 months. Restoring service cost about +9% per contact |
| Meta-analysis "no decay" | Not supported; it rests on four uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours |
| Varga & Holm "entirely an artifact" | Not supported, though their measurement critiques and the existence of some fading are confirmed |
| Mechanism | Meetings reduction is the leading measured pathway, roughly half the gain or possibly more. Fatigue is a smaller one. Replication outside these seven offices is still needed |
| Can reorganisation alone capture the gain? | Open. The control-office audit hints at partial yes. Answering it needs a trial with an arm that reorganises without cutting hours |

The most useful next study is the one the authors identify. It would randomise offices to three arms: a reduced-hours arm, a reorganisation arm with standard hours, and a control. It would ideally be run in a new employer, which would also serve as the out-of-sample replication of the meetings finding.
